original_value: AbstractIt can take several years to become proficient at direct ophthalmoscopy; the instrument’s single eyepiece allows only one individual to view the image at a time, which is considered disadvantageous during teaching. The introduction of smartphone ophthalmoscopes enables groups of teachers and students to view images together which could encourage peer-to-peer learning. In addition, the technology is significantly cheaper than the direct ophthalmoscope. User acceptability and engagement is essential to the success of any (medical) technological innovation. We sought to understand student opinions of a new commercially-available smartphone device for fundus examination, and compare usability to the traditional ophthalmoscope, from the perspective of both student practitioners and patients. Fifty-four undergraduate optometry students with prior experience of the traditional direct ophthalmoscope were asked to examine at least one eye with the D-EYE smartphone ophthalmoscope and also given an opportunity to experience the D-EYE from a patient’s perspective. Minimal instructions were provided and all examinations conducted through undilated pupils. Participants completed an opinion survey to feedback on aspects such as the ease of handling and working distance. Compared to the direct ophthalmoscope, 92% of students preferred the (longer) working distance of the D-EYE; 77% felt it was easier to handle; and 92% preferred the patient experience with the D-EYE. Despite the positive feedback, only 43% of students preferred the D-EYE when assuming the role of the practitioner. Free text responses indicated that students felt the D-EYE may be most useful as a teaching tool. Student opinions indicated that smartphone ophthalmoscopes are an effective training tool for students as an accompaniment to learning the traditional ophthalmoscope method.

result.paraphrase: It can take years to become skilled in direct ophthalmoscopy, and its single eyepiece permits only one person to view the image at once, a drawback in teaching. Smartphone ophthalmoscopes let teachers and students see images together, potentially promoting peer-to-peer learning, and they are much less expensive than direct ophthalmoscopes. Since user acceptability and engagement are crucial to the success of medical technologies, we aimed to assess student views of a new commercially available smartphone fundus examination device and compare its usability with the traditional ophthalmoscope from both student practitioner and patient perspectives. Fifty-four undergraduate optometry students who had previously used the direct ophthalmoscope examined at least one eye with the D-EYE smartphone ophthalmoscope and also experienced the D-EYE as patients. Only minimal instructions were given, and all examinations were performed through undilated pupils. Participants then completed a survey covering topics such as handling and working distance. Relative to the direct ophthalmoscope, 92% preferred the D-EYE’s longer working distance, 77% found it easier to handle, and 92% preferred the patient experience with the D-EYE. Even so, only 43% preferred the D-EYE when taking the practitioner role. Free-text comments suggested students saw the D-EYE as especially useful for teaching. Overall, student opinions showed smartphone ophthalmoscopes are an effective training aid alongside learning the traditional ophthalmoscope method.
